title: Little Ice Age
summary: A period of regionally cold conditions dated roughly 1300 to 1850, with its coldest phase from 1645 to 1715, during the Maunder Minimum. The evidence applies chiefly to Europe, and sources disagree on whether it was global. Reported effects include frozen rivers and Baltic Sea, advancing glaciers, crop failure and famine; Iceland lost about half its population.

uncertainty.note: Sources give the Little Ice Age as roughly AD 1300 to 1850 (EH.net) or approximately 1300 to 1850 (EBSCO), with a first phase beginning around 1290. EBSCO says estimates range from about 1350 or 1400 to 1850, and that it may have ended in the early 1700s.

as_recorded.value: a period of regionally cold conditions between roughly AD 1300 and 1850
coldest phase from 1645 to 1715, coinciding with the Maunder Minimum

where.modern_name: Iceland (marker only; a period of cooling across Europe and possibly worldwide)
where.historical_name: No single place; evidence concentrates in Europe and the North Atlantic, with Iceland among the hardest hit

importance.justification: A multi-century cooling that sources link to famine, glacier advance and social unrest.

reviewer_note: Boundaries are disputed: EBSCO says the evidence applies mainly to Europe and it could have been European only; EH.net calls the term questionable. The Iceland point is a marker with 5000 km uncertainty. Both sources are reference class; no scholarly paper opened. Tambora link is only thematic.
